entity_title: OIB: the number that unlocks everything
fact_text: The OIB (osobni identifikacijski broj) is Croatia's permanent personal identification number. Every public body and institution that keeps official records uses it to interconnect a person's data, so in practice you cannot open a bank account, sign a lease, be put on payroll or register for health insurance without one. Obtaining it is the first practical step of any move, even for EU free-movers.
evidence_quote: used by all competent authorities and legal persons with public authorities which keep official records (registers, lists and other records) on persons and assets, so that the official records can be interconnected

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed: as an EU citizen you can just start living and working in Croatia. Actually: almost every administrative and financial step is gated on having an OIB first. Action: obtain your OIB from the Tax Administration before attempting a bank account, lease or payroll.

entity_title: How an EU citizen gets an OIB
fact_text: A foreign natural person is assigned an OIB by a local office of the Tax Administration (Porezna uprava) once there is a cause to monitor them (e.g. incurred tax liability, acquiring assets, or registering in any official record). For an EU citizen the supporting document is a European identity card, and the Tax Administration issues the OIB within 8 days.
evidence_quote: Allocating and assigning of OIB to foreigners will be a priority for the Tax Administration and will be carried out within the time limit of 8 days.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed: the OIB is issued by the immigration/police office when you register residence. Actually: the Tax Administration (Porezna uprava) assigns the OIB, not the police. Action: apply for the OIB at a local Porezna uprava office (an EU ID card suffices).

entity_title: Get your OIB online before you arrive
fact_text: EU/EEA citizens do not have to appear in person to get an OIB: they can apply electronically through the e-Citizens (e-Građani) portal using the 'Electronic PIN (OIB) assignment' service via the e-Građani system. This lets you secure the OIB from abroad before landing, so a bank account or lease can be arranged on arrival.
evidence_quote: EU/EEA citizens can apply for PIN (OIB) also online via the e-Citizens portal, which is accessed via a credential: https://europe.gov.hr/en/

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed: you must be physically in Croatia at a tax office to get an OIB. Actually: EU/EEA citizens can request it online via the e-Citizens portal. Action: apply for the OIB online before you move so bank/lease steps aren't delayed.

fact_text: As an EEA national you may stay in Croatia for up to three months on nothing more than a valid ID card or passport, provided you are not an unreasonable burden on the social welfare system. There is no obligation to register this short-term stay with the police.
evidence_quote: EEA nationals are not obligated to register their short-term stay at a police administration or police station.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed: you must register with the authorities the moment you arrive. Actually: for the first three months an EU citizen needs only a valid ID and no registration. Action: don't rush the police visit on arrival, but diarise the 3-month mark because the obligation starts then.

fact_text: An EEA national intending to stay longer than three months must register their temporary stay on Form 1b at the police administration/station for their place of stay, no later than 8 days after the three-month period expires. This registration, not a visa or permit, is what legalises the longer stay.
evidence_quote: EEA nationals who intend to stay in the Republic of Croatia for more than 3 months are obligated to register their temporary stay (Form 1b) at the competent police administration/station according to their place of stay, no later than 8 days following the expiration of their 3-month stay.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed: free movement means EU citizens never have to register anywhere. Actually: past 3 months you must register temporary stay on Form 1b within 8 days. Action: file Form 1b at the local police administration as the 3-month mark passes.

entity_title: EU citizens get a certificate, not a residence permit
fact_text: When an EEA national registers their temporary stay, the police simply print a certificate confirming the registration, free of charge; there is no biometric residence-permit card as issued to non-EU nationals. That certificate is your proof of registered residence in Croatia.
evidence_quote: A certificate confirming that an EEA national has registered his temporary stay is printed out of the information system free of charge.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed: you'll receive a plastic residence-permit card like other immigrants. Actually: EU citizens get a printed registration certificate, issued free. Action: keep the certificate safe as your residence proof; don't wait for a permit card that won't come.

fact_text: An EEA national acquires the right to permanent stay in Croatia after five continuous years of legal residence. Time spent on registered temporary stay counts toward this five-year threshold.
evidence_quote: EEA nationals are entitled to permanent stay after five continuous years of legally staying in the Republic of Croatia.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed: permanent status needs a separate long application or naturalisation. Actually: EU citizens gain permanent stay after 5 continuous years of legal residence. Action: keep your temporary-stay registration continuous so the 5-year clock isn't reset.

entity_title: You must prove where you'll live to register
fact_text: Registering temporary stay as an EEA national requires documentary proof of accommodation, alongside a valid ID, proof of health insurance and proof of sufficient means of support. In practice this means having a signed lease or an owner's document for the address before you can complete residence registration.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed: you can register your stay first and sort housing out later. Actually: proof of accommodation is a required document for the registration itself. Action: secure a lease (or owner's consent) at your Croatian address before the police registration appointment.

entity_title: 183 days or centre of vital interests = Croatian tax resident
fact_text: Croatian tax law treats you as resident if you have a permanent or habitual residence in Croatia; habitual residence is a continuous or time-linked stay of at least 183 days across one or two calendar years. Residency is also decided by your centre of vital interests, meaning family, professional, economic and social ties.
evidence_quote: Habitual residence within the meaning of this Act shall be considered continuous or time-linked stay for at least 183 days in one or two calendar years.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed: EU free movement leaves your tax situation with your home country. Actually: about 183 days, or shifting your centre of vital interests to Croatia, makes you a Croatian tax resident (worldwide income). Action: track your days and get tax advice before crossing the threshold.

entity_title: Employment triggers compulsory HZZO health insurance
fact_text: Persons in an employment relationship working in the territory of Croatia are compulsorily insured under the mandatory health insurance system (HZZO). Your employer registers you and pays contributions; access to the public health system flows from that insured status, not from simply being an EU citizen.
evidence_quote: osobe u radnom odnosu službenici i namještenici i s njima, prema posebnim propisima izjednačene osobe zaposlene na državnom području Republike Hrvatske

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed: your EHIC or being an EU citizen covers you once you live in Croatia. Actually: public healthcare comes from HZZO insured status, which employment makes compulsory. Action: confirm your employer has filed your HZZO registration so you're covered from your first day of work.

entity_title: EHIC is for visits, not for living there
fact_text: The European Health Insurance Card (EHIC) only grants access to medically necessary, state-provided care during a temporary stay in another EU country. Once Croatia becomes your habitual residence you can no longer rely on your home EHIC: you register locally, using an S1 form if you remain insured elsewhere, otherwise joining HZZO.
evidence_quote: allows you to access medically necessary, state-provided healthcare while you are temporarily staying in any of the 27 EU countries, as well as Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, Switzerland, or the United Kingdom.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed: your home-country EHIC keeps covering you after you move. Actually: EHIC only covers temporary stays; on relocation you register locally (S1 form, or join HZZO). Action: don't rely on EHIC once you live in Croatia; arrange an S1 or HZZO registration.

entity_title: Your pension years in other EU states still count
fact_text: Under EU social-security coordination, a pension claim you submit in one member state is treated as submitted in every state where you completed insurance periods, and you can draw a pension from each state in which you were insured. Your Croatian and prior-country contribution years are aggregated rather than lost.
evidence_quote: Zahtjev podnesen u jednoj državi smatrat će se zahtjevom podnesenim u svim državama u kojima ste navršili razdoblja osiguranja.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed: moving countries means losing or separately chasing pension rights in each state. Actually: one claim counts across all states where you were insured, and periods are aggregated. Action: at retirement, file a single claim through your country-of-residence pension institution.

entity_title: Posted to Croatia? The A1 keeps you in home social security
fact_text: EU rules ensure a person moving within the EU is covered by the social-security legislation of only one member state at a time. If a home-country employer posts you to Croatia temporarily, an A1 certificate proves you remain under your home system, so no Croatian social contributions are due on that work.
evidence_quote: osigurati da osobe koje se kreću unutar EU-a budu obuhvaćene zakonodavstvom o socijalnoj sigurnosti samo jedne države članice te spriječiti da se na te osobe istovremeno primjenjuju zakonodavstva dviju ili više država članica

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed: working in Croatia always means paying Croatian social contributions. Actually: a posted worker with an A1 stays under the home country's system, since only one state's legislation applies. Action: if this is a posting, have the sending employer obtain an A1 before you start.

fact_text: Registration, change or de-registration in mandatory health insurance must be filed with HZZO within eight days of the event that creates, changes or ends the insurance basis (for example, starting a job). Insured status, and with it the right to use public healthcare, generally begins from the day the status is established.
evidence_quote: u roku od osam dana od dana nastanka, promjene ili prestanka okolnosti

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed: health cover is automatic once you're employed. Actually: the HZZO registration must be filed within 8 days of the triggering event, and cover runs from when status is established. Action: ensure the HZZO prijava is submitted within 8 days of your start date to avoid a coverage gap.
